cards.title: LRU Cache (Hash Map + Doubly Linked List)
cards.teaser: An LRU (Least-Recently-Used) cache evicts the oldest-accessed item when full. Combining a hash map with a doubly linked list gives O(1) get and O(1) put — the hash map finds the node instantly, the linked list tracks access order efficiently.

runs.text: keeps the most recently used items and discards the least recently used when capacity is exceeded. Two operations must both be O(1):
(insert or update, evicting if full). A single data structure cannot satisfy both — you need two working together.

items.text: — maps each key to its node in the linked list. O(1) lookup.
— orders nodes by recency. Head = most recent, tail = least recent. O(1) move-to-front and tail removal because each node has prev/next pointers.

explanation.code:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    """Python's OrderedDict already maintains insertion order
    and supports move_to_end — a clean built-in LRU."""

    def __init__(self, capacity: int) -> None:
        self.cap = capacity
        self.cache: OrderedDict[int, int] = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        self.cache.move_to_end(key)   # mark as most recently used
        return self.cache[key]

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.cache:
            self.cache.move_to_end(key)
        self.cache[key] = value
        if len(self.cache) > self.cap:
            self.cache.popitem(last=False)  # evict LRU (front)

# Usage
cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put(1, 10)
cache.put(2, 20)
cache.get(1)      # returns 10; key 1 is now MRU
cache.put(3, 30)  # evicts key 2 (LRU), inserts key 3
print(cache.get(2))  # -1 (evicted)

runs.text: ) use LRU eviction. CPU L1/L2 caches also use LRU or approximations of it. This exact design appears in nearly every system design interview involving caching.

Interview tip: when asked to implement LRU from scratch, use a doubly linked list (not singly) — you need to remove a middle node in O(1), which requires access to the previous node. Sentinel head/tail nodes eliminate edge-case null checks.

An LRU cache is like a whiteboard with limited space. Every time you use a fact, you erase it and rewrite it at the top. When the board fills up, you erase the bottom item (least recently used). The hash map is what lets you find any fact instantly without scanning the whole board. The linked list is what lets you cheaply move a fact to the top and drop one from the bottom.

cards.title: LFU Cache (Frequency Tracking + Double Hash Map)
cards.teaser: An LFU (Least-Frequently-Used) cache evicts the item accessed the fewest times — breaking ties by recency. It requires two hash maps and a frequency-ordered structure to achieve O(1) all operations.

runs.text: LFU is stricter than LRU: it evicts whatever has been accessed
overall, not just least recently. This requires tracking access frequency per key and being able to find the minimum-frequency group at O(1). The standard implementation uses:

items.text: — maps each key to its value and current frequency.
— maps each frequency to the ordered set of keys at that frequency (ordered by recency for tie-breaking).
— tracks the current minimum frequency so eviction is O(1).

runs.text: LFU is used when access patterns are skewed — a small set of very popular items dominates. LRU can evict a hot item if it wasn't accessed recently; LFU won't.
and uses a probabilistic frequency counter (Morris counter) rather than exact counts to save memory.

LFU has a cold-start problem: a newly inserted key starts at frequency 1 and is immediately vulnerable to eviction even if it's a frequently accessed item that just arrived. Redis addresses this with a decay mechanism — frequencies age over time so old-but-stale items don't persist forever.

LFU keeps a tally of how many times each item has been used. When eviction is needed, the item with the lowest tally gets dropped (with ties broken by 'which one was used least recently'). Implementing this at O(1) requires two hash maps: one to find any key's count instantly, one to find all keys at the minimum count instantly. The tricky part is updating the minimum count pointer after every access.

cards.title: Rate Limiter: Token Bucket
cards.teaser: The token bucket algorithm allows a burst up to a bucket capacity, then refills at a steady rate. Requests consume tokens; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected or queued. It smooths traffic while tolerating short bursts.

runs.text: controls how many requests a client can make in a time window. The

items.text: — maximum tokens the bucket can hold (burst allowance).
— tokens added per second (sustained throughput limit).
consumes one token. If none available, reject (HTTP 429) or queue.

explanation.code:
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity: float, refill_rate: float) -> None:
        """capacity: max tokens; refill_rate: tokens/second."""
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.refill_rate = refill_rate
        self.tokens = capacity          # start full
        self.last_refill = time.monotonic()

    def _refill(self) -> None:
        now = time.monotonic()
        elapsed = now - self.last_refill
        new_tokens = elapsed * self.refill_rate
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + new_tokens)
        self.last_refill = now

    def allow(self) -> bool:
        """Returns True if the request is allowed."""
        self._refill()
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False   # bucket empty — rate limit exceeded

# Example: 10 req/s sustained, burst up to 20
limiter = TokenBucket(capacity=20, refill_rate=10)
for i in range(25):
    result = "OK" if limiter.allow() else "RATE LIMITED"
    print(f"Request {i+1}: {result}")
# Requests 1-20: OK (burst); 21-25: RATE LIMITED

runs.text: In distributed systems, the token state must live in a shared store.
is commonly used: a Lua script atomically reads the current token count, computes refill, and decrements — all in one round trip.
all use token bucket or variants internally.

Token bucket vs leaky bucket: the token bucket allows bursts (up to capacity) and processes requests whenever tokens are available. The leaky bucket outputs at a fixed rate regardless of input — it's a FIFO queue draining at constant speed. Token bucket is more common for APIs because bursts are often legitimate.

Imagine a vending machine that gives out tickets at a rate of 10 per second but can hold up to 20 at once. If you walk up and want 15 tickets immediately, fine — you get them all (burst). But if you keep asking, you have to wait for new tickets to accumulate. The bucket fills slowly and steadily; you drain it fast. This is token bucket: bursts are OK, sustained overdrive is not.

cards.title: Rate Limiter: Sliding Window (Timestamps in Deque)
cards.teaser: The sliding window rate limiter stores a deque of request timestamps per client. On each request, it removes timestamps older than the window and checks if the count exceeds the limit — precise but memory-proportional to request count.

runs.text: Unlike fixed windows (which reset at clock boundaries and allow burst across the seam), a
counts requests in the most recent N seconds from
, not from a clock tick. This eliminates the boundary-burst problem at the cost of storing individual timestamps.

explanation.code:
import time
from collections import deque

class SlidingWindowRateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, max_requests: int, window_seconds: float) -> None:
        self.max_requests = max_requests
        self.window = window_seconds
        # Per-client timestamp log
        self.log: dict[str, deque[float]] = {}

    def allow(self, client_id: str) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        if client_id not in self.log:
            self.log[client_id] = deque()

        timestamps = self.log[client_id]
        cutoff = now - self.window

        # Drop timestamps outside the current window
        while timestamps and timestamps[0] <= cutoff:
            timestamps.popleft()

        if len(timestamps) < self.max_requests:
            timestamps.append(now)
            return True

        return False   # window is full — rate limited

# 5 requests per 10 seconds per client
limiter = SlidingWindowRateLimiter(max_requests=5, window_seconds=10)
client = "user-42"
for i in range(7):
    ok = limiter.allow(client)
    print(f"Request {i+1}: {'OK' if ok else 'BLOCKED'}")
# First 5: OK; 6-7: BLOCKED

runs.text: ) approximates this by interpolating between two fixed-window counts — far more memory-efficient. For a window of 60 seconds, store only two counters instead of up to 60 timestamps per client.

items.text: — O(1) per request (amortized), memory O(max_requests) per client. Precise.
— O(1) per request, memory O(1) per client. Off by at most ~0.5% in practice.

runs.text: In Redis, implement the deque with a sorted set (ZSET): timestamps are scores, so ZREMRANGEBYSCORE trims old entries and ZCARD counts current ones. A single Lua script makes the check-and-add atomic. This is the pattern used by many API gateway middleware layers.

A sliding window rate limiter keeps a log of when each request arrived. When a new request comes in, it looks back exactly N seconds and counts how many requests are in that window. If too many, it blocks; otherwise it logs the new timestamp and allows it. The deque is the right data structure because you only ever remove from the front (old timestamps) and add to the back (new timestamps).

cards.title: Bloom Filter
cards.teaser: A Bloom filter is a probabilistic bit array that answers 'definitely not in set' or 'probably in set' — never false negatives, but controlled false positives. Space is O(m) bits for m-bit array; lookup and insert are O(k) hash operations.

runs.text: uses a bit array of size m and k independent hash functions. To insert an element, set the k bit positions determined by the k hashes. To query, check if all k positions are set — if any bit is 0, the element is
; if all are 1, the element is
(false positive possible due to hash collisions across different elements).

items.text: — each SSTable has a Bloom filter to avoid disk seeks for keys that don't exist in that SSTable.
— stores malicious URLs in a Bloom filter for safe browsing checks before hitting the server.
— RedisBloom module provides a native Bloom filter command set.
— check if a URL has been crawled without a full DB lookup.

runs.text: Bloom filters cannot delete elements — setting bits to 0 might erase bits shared with other elements. If deletion is needed, use a Counting Bloom Filter (each position stores a counter instead of a single bit), at 4-8x the memory cost.

A Bloom filter is like a very compact checklist. When you add an item, you put checkmarks in several spots (determined by hashing the item). When you query, you check those same spots. If any spot is empty, the item was never added — guaranteed. If all spots are checked, the item was probably added — but another item might have accidentally checked all those same spots, giving a false positive. The trade-off: use kilobytes instead of megabytes, accept a small lie rate of 'probably yes'.

cards.title: Count-Min Sketch
cards.teaser: Count-Min Sketch estimates the frequency of any element in a stream using a 2D array of counters and multiple hash functions. It overestimates but never underestimates, uses sub-linear memory, and powers heavy-hitter detection in analytics pipelines.

runs.text: (CMS) is a probabilistic frequency table. It has d rows and w columns (d independent hash functions, w buckets each). To increment an element's count, hash it with each of the d functions and increment one cell per row. To query, take the
across all d rows — the minimum is the best estimate because all errors are overcounting from hash collisions.

Space: O(d × w), independent of the number of distinct elements. Error bound: with probability 1 - δ, the estimate is within ε × N of the true count, where d = ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉ and w = ⌈e/ε⌉. Real-world uses:

items.text: — heavy-hitter detection (top trending topics, most accessed URLs).
— the RedisBloom module includes a CMS implementation.
— count packet frequencies per IP in a router with fixed SRAM.

runs.text: CMS vs exact counting: exact frequency counting with a hash map uses O(distinct elements) memory. For a log stream with billions of events and millions of distinct URLs, that's gigabytes. CMS uses kilobytes for the same stream with bounded error — the canonical space-accuracy trade-off.

Count-Min Sketch is like counting votes using several overlapping ballot boxes. Each item you add gets one tally mark in each of several boxes (determined by hashing). When you ask 'how many votes did X get?', you look at X's slot in every box and take the smallest number — because collisions only inflate counts, never shrink them. The smallest across all boxes is the closest estimate. More boxes mean fewer wrong tallies, but more memory.

cards.title: HyperLogLog (Cardinality Estimation)
cards.teaser: HyperLogLog estimates the count of distinct elements (cardinality) in a stream using O(log log N) bits per register, with ~2% error. It powers 'unique visitors' metrics in every major analytics system without storing the elements themselves.

runs.text: Counting exact distinct elements requires O(N) memory (store all of them).

answers 'approximately how many distinct items?' using only a few kilobytes regardless of stream size. The core intuition: hash each element uniformly, then track the maximum number of leading zeros seen across all hashes. More leading zeros statistically implies more distinct elements.
In practice, HLL splits the stream across m sub-streams (using the first few bits of the hash) and maintains one register per sub-stream. The
of the estimates across registers reduces variance. Final estimate:
, where M_i is the max leading zeros in register i and α_m is a bias-correction constant.

explanation.code:
# Conceptual sketch — production uses the full HLL++ algorithm
import hashlib
import math

class HyperLogLog:
    def __init__(self, b: int = 10) -> None:
        """b bits for register index → 2^b registers."""
        self.b = b
        self.m = 1 << b        # number of registers
        self.registers = [0] * self.m
        self.alpha = 0.7213 / (1 + 1.079 / self.m)   # bias constant

    def add(self, item: str) -> None:
        h = int(hashlib.sha256(item.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
        idx = h >> (256 - self.b)               # first b bits → register
        remaining = h & ((1 << (256 - self.b)) - 1)
        # Count leading zeros in remaining bits (+1)
        rho = (256 - self.b) - remaining.bit_length() + 1
        self.registers[idx] = max(self.registers[idx], rho)

    def count(self) -> int:
        z = sum(2 ** -r for r in self.registers)
        raw = self.alpha * self.m * self.m / z
        return round(raw)

# Demo
hll = HyperLogLog(b=10)   # 1024 registers, ~1.5 KB
for i in range(1_000_000):
    hll.add(f"user:{i}")
print(f"Distinct estimate: {hll.count():,}")  # ~1,000,000 ±2%

items.text: commands use HLL natively. Stores up to 2^64 distinct elements in 12 KB.
— cardinality aggregation for unique visitor counts in dashboards.

runs.text: HLL registers are mergeable — you can split a stream across machines, compute per-shard HLL registers, then merge them by taking the max per register position. This makes HLL ideal for distributed 'unique users across all shards' queries with a single aggregation step.

HyperLogLog exploits randomness: if you flip a fair coin until you get heads, seeing 10 tails in a row is rare — it suggests you flipped a lot of coins. HLL hashes each element (making it look like a random bit string), then tracks the longest run of leading zeros seen. A long run statistically implies many distinct elements. Using many independent sub-streams and averaging reduces the error to about 2% while using only kilobytes of memory.

cards.title: Skip List
cards.teaser: A skip list is a probabilistic sorted linked list with express lanes — multiple levels of forward pointers let search, insert, and delete run in O(log n) expected time. Redis uses skip lists for its sorted set (ZSET) implementation.

runs.text: is a hierarchy of sorted linked lists. Level 0 is a full linked list of all elements. Each higher level is a randomly sampled subset of the level below — on average every other element. Searching starts at the top level and works downward, skipping large ranges quickly.

Each node is promoted to level k with probability p^k (typically p = 0.5). Expected height of the skip list is O(log n). This randomness eliminates the need for complex rebalancing rotations required by AVL or Red-Black trees — a major implementation simplicity advantage.
Why Redis chose skip lists over balanced BSTs for sorted sets:

items.text: — no rotation logic; probabilistic balance is easy to audit.
— once you find the start of a range at level 0, traversal is a simple linked list walk. BSTs require an in-order traversal.
— skip lists admit concurrent lock-free implementations more naturally than trees.

runs.text: Redis ZSET: when a sorted set has more than 128 elements or any element exceeds 64 bytes, Redis switches from a ziplist (compact encoding) to a skip list backed by a hash table. ZADD, ZRANK, ZRANGEBYSCORE all run in O(log n) via the skip list.

A skip list is a sorted linked list with express lanes. The bottom lane has every element; the lane above skips roughly half of them; the lane above that skips half again. To search, you ride the top express lane until you overshoot, drop down a level, continue, repeat. It's like taking the highway, then local roads, then your street. The express lanes are built randomly — promoting each element by coin flip — so no rebalancing is ever needed.

cards.title: Distributed Hash Table (Chord / Kademlia)
cards.teaser: A Distributed Hash Table (DHT) stores key-value pairs across many nodes with no central coordinator. Each node is responsible for a key range; lookups route through O(log n) hops. Chord uses a ring; Kademlia uses XOR distance — both power peer-to-peer systems.

runs.text: solves: 'given a cluster of N machines, which machine stores key K?' without a central directory. The answer must be consistent even as nodes join and leave.
maps nodes and keys onto a circular identifier space (a ring of 2^m positions using SHA-1). Each node maintains a
of m shortcuts to successors at exponential distances. Lookup routes in O(log n) hops: each hop halves the remaining distance.

) uses XOR as the distance metric between node IDs. XOR distance is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality, allowing routing tables (k-buckets) to be built and traversed in O(log n) hops with better churn resilience than Chord.

DHTs enable decentralized storage at scale: DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing (a simpler DHT variant) to assign key ranges to nodes. The difference from Chord: Cassandra uses virtual nodes and a coordinator model rather than full O(log n) routing — trading decentralization for operational simplicity.

A DHT is a phone book distributed across many nodes, where every node knows a shortcut to nodes at exponential distances. To look up a key, you hash it to get an address on the ring, then ask your neighbor who's closest to that address. They ask their neighbor who's closer still — like a treasure hunt where each clue is closer to the treasure. After O(log n) hops, you reach the node that owns the key. This scales to millions of nodes with no central server.

cards.title: Merkle Tree
cards.teaser: A Merkle tree is a binary tree of cryptographic hashes where each parent is the hash of its children. The root hash summarizes the entire dataset — any single-byte change cascades up to a different root. Used in Git, blockchains, and distributed data sync.

runs.text: is built bottom-up: leaf nodes hold hashes of data blocks; internal nodes hold hashes of their children's hashes. The
is a single hash that represents the entire dataset. Verifying that a specific data block belongs to the dataset requires only O(log n) hashes — the path from leaf to root (a

items.text: — every commit object references a tree object (a Merkle tree of file hashes). Two commits sharing the same tree hash have identical file contents, enabling fast diffing and deduplication.
— block headers store the Merkle root of all transactions. SPV clients can verify a transaction with O(log n) hashes without downloading the full block.
— anti-entropy repair uses Merkle trees to compare key ranges between replicas and sync only the diverging subtrees.
— content-addressable storage: every file chunk is identified by its hash, and larger files are represented as Merkle DAGs.

runs.text: A Merkle proof is a list of sibling hashes from leaf to root. Given a leaf value and its proof, anyone can recompute the root and verify it matches the trusted root — without seeing any other data. This is how blockchain light clients and certificate transparency logs work.

A Merkle tree is a verification pyramid. At the bottom, hash every data chunk individually. Then hash pairs of hashes together to form the next layer up. Repeat until one root hash remains. Change any data chunk, and its hash changes, which changes its parent's hash, all the way up to the root. Two databases with the same Merkle root are guaranteed to have identical data — without comparing any actual records. And you can prove any single chunk belongs with just the hashes of its siblings on the path to the root.

cards.title: Consistent Hashing Ring
cards.teaser: Consistent hashing distributes keys across nodes by placing both keys and nodes on a circular hash ring. Adding or removing a node only remaps O(K/N) keys instead of O(K) — essential for horizontal scaling in distributed caches and databases.

runs.text: assigns keys to nodes. But if N changes (a node is added or removed), nearly every key remaps — catastrophic for a cache where every remapped key is a cache miss.

maps both keys and nodes to a [0, 2^32) ring using the same hash function. Each key is owned by the first node clockwise from its ring position. When a node is added, it only steals keys from its immediate clockwise successor.
Virtual nodes (replicas per physical node) ensure even key distribution — without them, the physical nodes land unevenly on the ring and some carry much more load. Used in:

items.text: — each node owns token ranges on a ring; virtual nodes (vnodes) allow flexible rebalancing.
— consistent hashing partitions data across storage nodes.
— libmemcached and twemproxy use consistent hashing to route cache requests to a pool of Memcached servers.
— session-sticky load balancing: same client always routes to same backend (if using the client IP or session token as the key).

runs.text: The math: with N nodes and K keys, adding or removing one node remaps exactly K/N keys on average — the minimum theoretically possible. Naive modular hashing remaps (N-1)/N of all keys when N changes by 1.

Imagine a clock face representing all possible hash values. Place your cache servers at random positions on the clock. To store a key, hash it to a clock position and walk clockwise until you hit a server — that server owns the key. When you add a new server, it only steals keys from the next server clockwise. Remove a server, and its keys move to the next server clockwise. Only a small fraction of keys move each time — that's what makes it 'consistent'.

cards.title: Inverted Index (Full-Text Search)
cards.teaser: An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it — the reverse of a document-to-terms mapping. It's the core data structure powering every search engine, from Elasticsearch to PostgreSQL full-text search.

runs.text: maps document → list of terms. An

flips this: term → list of (document, positions). This inversion is what makes full-text search fast: a query for 'distributed systems' hashes to two term lookups and intersects two posting lists — instead of scanning every document.

items.text: — doc IDs stored as deltas (gaps), then compressed with variable-byte or SIMD-friendly encoding (PFOR). Elasticsearch uses Lucene's FOR-delta compression.
— rank by how frequently the term appears in the document vs how rare it is across all documents.
— use position lists to verify 'distributed systems' appears as a consecutive phrase, not just as two separate words.
— Elasticsearch distributes index shards across nodes; each shard is a complete Lucene index.

runs.text: Time complexity: indexing is O(total tokens across all documents). AND query intersection is O(min posting list length) with galloping (exponential) search to skip ahead in the longer list. OR query is a merge of sorted posting lists in O(total results). This is why full-text search is fast even over billions of documents.

An inverted index is like the index at the back of a textbook. Instead of reading every page to find where 'hash table' appears, you look up 'hash table' in the index and it immediately tells you pages 45, 67, and 102. Build this index for every word in every document, and search becomes a series of lookups rather than a scan. The 'inverted' part means the mapping goes term → documents, not document → terms.
